rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The Boltzmann constant k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K links macroscopic temperature to microscopic molecular energy. RMS speed v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M) characterizes the typical molecular speed in a gas at temperature T. At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster; v_rms determines diffusion rates, effusion, and kinetic energy.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Boltzmann constant: $k = \frac{R}{N_A} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J/K}$
RMS speed: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$
Most probable speed: $v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2kT}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Ideal Gas Assumption: Formulas assume point particles with elastic collisions and no intermolecular forces. Real gases deviate at high P or low T.  ·  Thermal Equilibrium Required: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and well-defined v_rms apply only at equilibrium. Non-equilibrium flows have different velocity distributions.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Statement 1: Boltzmann constant relates temperature to average molecular kinetic energy via ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT.  ·  Statement 2: RMS speed is the square root of the mean of squared molecular speeds, not the arithmetic mean speed.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Confusing v_rms with average speed: v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) ≠ ⟨v⟩. They differ by ~8% for Maxwellian gases.  ·  Using M in g/mol instead of kg/mol: Must convert to SI (kg/mol) for v_rms in m/s.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Boltzmann Constant Definition: k = R/N_A where R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Value: k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K (exact since 2019 SI redefinition). It converts temperature (kelvin) into energy (joules) per particle.  ·  Physical Significance of k: Average translational KE per molecule = (3/2)kT. At 300 K, ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)(1.38×10⁻²³)(300) ≈ 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J ≈ 0.039 eV. This is the thermal energy scale governing molecular motion.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: v_rms = √(3RT/M): plug T in K, M in kg/mol, R = 8.314.  ·  Same T → same ⟨KE⟩; lighter = faster.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Define Boltzmann constant and state its value with units.  ·  Q2. Derive the expression for rms speed of gas molecules.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Calculate v_rms numerically: convert M to kg/mol (e.g., O₂ = 0.032 kg/mol).  ·  Compare speeds of two gases at same T using v₁/v₂ = √(M₂/M₁).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K bridges macroscopic T and microscopic energy.  ·  v_rms = √(3RT/M): depends on T and M, not on P or V directly.  ·  At same T, all gases have same ⟨KE⟩ but different v_rms.  ·  v_rms > v_avg > v_mp always for Maxwellian distribution.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Ludwig Boltzmann (1844–1906) established statistical mechanics; his constant was named posthumously.  ·  The 2019 SI redefinition fixed k exactly, making the kelvin dependent on the joule rather than water's triple point.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Calculate v_rms for helium at 400 K. (M = 4 g/mol)  ·  Q4. Compare rms speeds of H₂ and CO₂ at the same temperature.  ·  Q5. State Graham's law of effusion and explain it using kinetic theory.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Explain why hydrogen escapes Earth's atmosphere but nitrogen does not.  ·  Derive v_rms from P = (1/3)ρv²_rms and PV = nRT.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: At what T does N₂ have v_rms = 1000 m/s? T = Mv²/(3R) = 0.028×10⁶/(3×8.314) ≈ 1123 K.  ·  Graham's law: H₂ effuses √(32/2) = 4 times faster than O₂ through a pinhole at same T and P.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Boltzmann constant k equals: → B  ·  At the same temperature, which gas has the highest rms speed? → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: RMS Speed Formula: v_rms = √(⟨v²⟩) = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M), where m = molecular mass, M = molar mass. Derived from equating pressure expression P = (1/3)ρv²_rms with ideal gas law PV = nRT.  ·  Speed Hierarchy: For Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: v_mp = √(2kT/m) < v_avg = √(8kT/πm) < v_rms = √(3kT/m). Numerical ratio: v_mp : v_avg : v_rms ≈ 1.41 : 1.60 : 1.73 (or 1 : 1.13 : 1.22 normalized to v_mp).  ·  Temperature Dependence: v_rms ∝ √T. Doubling absolute temperature increases v_rms by factor √2 ≈ 1.414. Cooling to 1/4 original T halves the rms speed.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Average speed: $v_{avg} = \sqrt{\frac{8kT}{\pi m}} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$  ·  Average KE per molecule: $\langle KE \rangle = \frac{3}{2} kT$  ·  Speed ratio: $v_{mp} : v_{avg} : v_{rms} = \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{8/\pi} : \sqrt{3}$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Translational Motion Only: v_rms refers to center-of-mass translational speed. Rotational and vibrational energies contribute to total internal energy but not to v_rms.  ·  Classical Regime: Quantum effects become significant when de Broglie wavelength λ = h/(mv) approaches interparticle spacing. For most gases above ~10 K, classical treatment is valid.  ·  Lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Graham's law of effusion follows directly from v_rms ∝ 1/√M.  ·  Thinking heavier gases have higher KE at same T: All gases at same T have identical ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT regardless of mass.  ·  Believing v_rms depends on pressure: v_rms depends only on T and M for ideal gases; P affects density, not individual molecular speeds.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Assuming all molecules move at v_rms: Individual speeds vary widely; v_rms is a statistical measure of the distribution.  ·  Since 2019, k is defined exactly as 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K, fixing the kelvin in terms of energy.  ·  v_rms appears in pressure formula because pressure depends on ⟨v²⟩, not ⟨v⟩².

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Escape velocity criterion: if v_rms > v_escape/6, significant atmospheric loss occurs over geological time.  ·  NEB frequently asks numerical calculation of v_rms given T and M — ensure M in kg/mol.  ·  Statement 3: At identical temperatures, gases with lower molar mass have higher rms speeds.
